forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Tendring's main budget was £3.669m underspent against profile at end of July 2026, papers show
news_drafts.lead:
Tendring Council's General Fund Revenue Account was underspent by £3.669m against its profiled budget at the end of July 2026, according to a budget monitoring report (the in-year check of spending against budget) for the Cabinet meeting of 23 October. The General Fund is the account that council tax and business rates pay into, covering services other than council housing and schools.

A profiled budget is the annual budget spread across the months of the year, so the figure compares actual spending with what the council had planned to have spent by the end of July. The report describes the £3.669m as a net underspend, meaning the total after overspends and underspends on individual budgets are set against each other.

The report says the position reflects the timing of spending across budgets and the timing of Government reimbursements for housing benefit. It does not present the figure as a saving, and the papers give no full-year forecast alongside it.

findings.headline: The Operations and Delivery variance of (864,706) to profile is attributed in part to homelessness budgets, which the paper says continue to be supported by Government grant funding
findings.detail: The paper says a number of positive actions have been taken and will continue to respond to associated demand, and that the position will remain under review for the rest of the year.
findings.matters: Homelessness cost pressures funded by government grant are a demand pressure that finance officers at other councils are tracking, and the grant dependence is what a lender would ask about.
findings.figures: Operations and Delivery: full year 20,891,488, profiled 5,165,206, actual 4,300,499, variance (864,706)
findings.quote: which continue to be supported by Government Grant funding contributions

findings.headline: £337k of conservation S106 income is recorded as needing to be spent by March 2027
findings.detail: The table shows 337 (£'000) of conservation S106 money to be spent within one year. The footnote says it relates to the Harwich Area, with an update planned for the Q2 report. A further 758 (£'000) of affordable housing S106 money is shown as held for four years or more.
findings.matters: A spend-by date on a fixed sum is a deadline a finance director has to meet or explain, and held S106 balances over four years are a reserve-like position other councils also manage.
findings.figures: Conservation: 337 (less than 1 year); Affordable Housing: 758 (4 years +); total S106 by time band 337 / 76 / 87 / 2,742 (£'000)
findings.quote: To be spent by March 2027 - relates to the Harwich Area

findings.headline: General debt collected to date is 77.20% at Quarter 1 2026/27, against 82.86% at Quarter 1 2025/26
findings.detail: Council tax is at 36.87% against 36.98% in the 2025/26 Quarter 1 figure, and housing rents are at 96.57% against 96.42%. The paper says no accurate business rates information is available for the period because of technical issues with a third-party system.
findings.matters: A lower general debt collection rate at the same point in the year is a cash-flow pressure a finance director tracks, and the missing business rates figure is a gap the reader needs to know about.
findings.figures: General debt Q1 2025/26 82.86%, Q1 2026/27 77.20%; Council tax 36.87%; Housing rents 96.57%

findings.headline: Total investments rise from £97,642k at 1 April to £125,970k at the end of July 2026
findings.detail: The paper attributes the increase to the timing of the Council's cash flow and the receipt of Government grants. Investments were held with four counterparties, including two money market funds, at the end of the period.
findings.matters: A rise in cash balances of this size is a liquidity position a lender and another council's treasury team would both want to see, with the cause given as timing.
findings.figures: Opening 97,642; invested to date 700,348; repaid to date 672,020; balance 125,970 (£'000)

findings.headline: HRA financing costs are shown at 40.67% of net revenue stream in the current 2026/27 forecast, falling to 36.87% by 2028/29
findings.detail: The original 2026/27 estimate was 40.87%. The forecasts are 37.92% for 2027/28 and 36.87% for 2028/29. The General Fund ratio is 1.04% for 2026/27 and the total is 41.71% in the current forecast.
findings.matters: An HRA financing cost ratio above 40% of net revenue stream is a figure a lender and any council with a similar HRA will examine closely, and the forecast fall is the trajectory they will ask about.
findings.figures: HRA: original 40.87%, current forecast 40.67%, 2027/28 37.92%, 2028/29 36.87%; General Fund 1.04%; total 41.71% current forecast
findings.quote: Actual Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream (%) 40.87% 40.67% 37.92% 36.87%
